frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d3: Joseph Davies, serving as President Roosevelt's special representative, reported to the President and the Secretary of State on May 21, 1943. Davies was then on a sensitive mission to Moscow, carrying word to Stalin in person. His account is Document 3 of the Cairo and Tehran volume in the Foreign Relations series. What he reported must be taken from the text itself; the catalog record supplies the mission, the date, and the men who received it.
frus-1944-quebec-d3:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote again to President Roosevelt on March 21, 1944, the day after Roosevelt's reply. The State Department printed the message in its Quebec 1944 volume, where the pre-conference letters build toward the September meeting.

Churchill rarely let a subject rest with one letter, and March 1944 gave him urgent material: the Italian campaign, the coming invasion, and relations with France and Russia. A next-day follow-up shows him pressing his case while the exchange was hot. For readers, the message is evidence of how the alliance's business was done: personally, in writing, and at a pace set by the Prime Minister's pen.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d3: Answering his ambassador the same day, President Roosevelt wrote to Averell Harriman in Moscow on 18 July 1944. The reply is document 3 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. Paired with Harriman's report beside it, the message lets readers follow both ends of a presidential exchange about Soviet affairs in the summer of 1944.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d3:
Invite him together, at the same moment: Churchill pressed his plan in a telegram to Truman of May 11, 1945. The two should offer Stalin a joint invitation to an agreed, unshattered town in Germany, for a tripartite meeting in July. They should not meet at any place inside the present Russian military zone. Twice running, Churchill notes, we have come to meet him.

He adds a warning about time. The Russians, he writes, are concerned about the Western allies now, because of their civilization and tools of war. That concern would shrink once the Western armies dispersed. Britain's election, whenever held, should not govern duty. An invitation from the King to visit England closes the wire.
tob-0038-d3:
Book III of the Church Committee's 1976 report holds the supplementary detailed staff reports that back the main findings. These are the working papers of the Senate inquiry into American intelligence. They run case by case and program by program.

Staff investigators lay out the evidence on covert action, assassination plots, mail opening, and domestic operations, with documents and names attached. Readers who doubt a summary claim can check the record here. For historians, this book is the deep archive behind the headlines, the place where the great inquiry shows its proof.
tob-0039-d3:
Roll 4 of the Doctors' Trial microfilm carries forward the verbatim record from Nuremberg, where an American military tribunal sat in 1946 and 1947. The defendants were doctors and health officials of the Third Reich. The charge sheet tied them to experiments in the camps.

Here the court hears more of the evidence by which the world first learned, in sworn form, what camp medicine had done. Survivors, documents, and expert voices enter the record in turn. The roll has no narrative voice of its own; its power lies in accumulation. Kept complete, the transcript set lets researchers test every later account of the trial against the words spoken at the time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d3:
William Donovan, director of the Office of Strategic Services, wrote to President Truman on 25 August 1945. Donovan had built the OSS, America's wartime spy and sabotage service, from nothing in 1942. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Donovan spent 1945 urging Truman to keep a strong central intelligence service in peace, under his own vision of how it should run. This memorandum is part of that campaign, sent weeks before the president chose a different course. Readers meet the founding argument of American central intelligence in its author's own hand: bold, urgent, and, in the short run, unsuccessful. The rest of the volume is, in part, the story of what replaced it.
frus-1861-d3:
William H. Seward, the new Secretary of State, sent a general letter to all American ministers abroad on 9 March 1861. It is document 3 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward had taken office only days before, under President Abraham Lincoln. His first task abroad was to keep foreign powers from backing the new Confederacy. A circular order let him set that line at every post at the same time, before local habits could form. Lincoln had been in office five days, and his voice now spoke in Seward's pen. Five days in office had set the tone.
frus-1862-d3:
From his post abroad, Charles Francis Adams wrote to William H. Seward on 29 November 1861. It stands as Document 3 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the autumn of the war's first year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d3:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 November 1862, the same day as his letter that opens the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 3 in part one of the 1863 Foreign Relations volume.

Two reports in one day show a post with more news than one sheet could hold. Adams wrote on the British government's mood, the press, and the state of the war as London saw it. His mail was the State Department's best source on the power that could still tip the war. This letter is part of that flow at its source.
